story: Day 1 of 12: 54,248 Texans have voted early (10 in person, 54,238 by mail), 0.3% of registered voters.
Turnout is behind 2022's pace: 61% fewer ballots than on the same day in 2022, after adjusting for registration growth.

Today so far: 10 in-person votes from 1 of 254 counties. In those counties that is 96% fewer than the same day in 2022 (10 vs. 235, adjusted for registration). Counties that have not posted today are compared with 2022 through yesterday.
Against 2018, the last high-turnout midterm, the 30 largest counties are 76% behind the same day.
Strongest turnout vs. 2022: Harris (-20%), Dallas (-20%), Tarrant (-32%). Weakest: Fort Bend (-94%), Collin (-83%), Williamson (-80%).
The four big blue counties are at 70% of their 2022 pace; rural Texas is at 6%. That gap favors Democrats.

What it means: if each county's ballots split the way the county is expected to vote (with mail leaning Democratic), the early vote so far is about Hinojosa +27.0. Spread across counties the way 2022 was, the same ballots would be about Hinojosa +9.9, so this year's mix is 17.1 points better for Hinojosa (roughly 9,277 net votes).
Not reported yet: Bexar, El Paso, Hidalgo, Brazoria, Parker, Guadalupe and others. These are left out of the comparisons until they post numbers.

Early votes lean Democratic in Texas cities and mail ballots lean Democratic in Harris, so an early Democratic lead is expected and shrinks once Election Day votes are added. Turnout shows where votes come from, not whom they are for.
